passages.t: David goes over to the Philistines
passages.happening:
David says to himself, “One of these days now I will be swept away by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than to escape to the land of the Philistines” (verse 1). Then Saul will stop searching for him, and he will slip out of Saul's hand.

So David goes with his six hundred men to Achish king of Gath. They settle there, each man with his family, and David with his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail (verses 2-3). When Saul hears that David has fled to Gath, he stops searching for him (verse 4).

David asks Achish for a place in one of the country towns, ‘For why should your servant live in the royal city with you?’ (verse 5). ‘That day Achish gave him Ziklag, and to this day it still belongs to the kings of Judah’ (verse 6). David lives in Philistine territory for a year and four months (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The chapter follows straight on from Saul's parting words in chapter 26, that David would surely prevail, and it is striking how little they reassure David. He speaks only to himself, not to God. In chapter 23 he asked the LORD again and again. Here there is no prayer, no priest, no ephod and no word from God. He decides out of exhaustion that his only safety is to leave Israel.

He has been to Achish before, and escaped only by pretending to be mad. Now he comes as the captain of a private army.

Mercenary service was common in that world. Kings valued experienced soldiers with no local ties, and a band like David's, fighters with their families and flocks, could be settled on the frontier in return for military service and a share of the plunder. A town of his own suited both men. Achish gained a guard on his southern border, and David gained freedom from close watching.

Ziklag lay somewhere in the western Negev, the dry southern country. Just where is debated. The note that Ziklag still belongs to the kings of Judah ‘to this day’ shows that the writer lived after the kingdom divided, around 930 BC.

The move works. Saul stops hunting him. But it traps David in a double life.
passages.later:
A psalm headed for David's time at Gath says what David did not say here: ‘When I am afraid, I put my trust in You’ (Psalm 56:3).

Chronicles remembers the warriors who joined him there: ‘these were the men who came to David at Ziklag, while he was still banished from the presence of Saul son of Kish’ (1 Chronicles 12:1).
passages.asks: David said to himself that one day Saul would get him, and made his plans without asking God. Ask what decisions you have made in exhaustion or fear without praying about them. And ask what promises of God you have stopped repeating to yourself.

passages.happening:
David and his men raid the Geshurites, the Girzites and the Amalekites, peoples who had lived in the land toward Shur and Egypt from ancient times (verse 8). Whenever he attacks, he leaves no man or woman alive, and takes the flocks and herds, donkeys, camels and clothing (verse 9).

When he comes back, Achish asks, “What have you raided today?” David names places in the south of Judah, or the lands of Judah's allied clans (verse 10). He leaves no one alive to be brought to Gath, saying they would report what he had really done. ‘And this was David’s custom the whole time he lived in Philistine territory’ (verse 11).

‘So Achish trusted David’ (verse 12). He thinks that David has made himself so hated by Israel that he will be Achish's servant forever.
passages.hearers:
The chapter is short and cool in tone. The narrator reports and does not weigh. It is built on the gap between what David does and what he says.

The peoples David raids were half-wandering groups of the southern desert toward Shur, on the border of Egypt. These southern Geshurites are different from the kingdom of Geshur in the north. The Jerahmeelites and Kenites, whose lands David pretends to have raided, were clans closely tied to Judah. That is why Achish believes the raids have made David hated by his own people.

Raiding for livestock and goods was a normal part of life on the desert's edge, and the Amalekites were remembered in Israel as old enemies. But the reason David leaves no one alive is given plainly: secrecy. No one must survive to tell Achish where he has really been.

The word for David's custom is the word usually translated justice. The future king who will be responsible for justice in Israel has, for now, a custom of killing witnesses.

Achish trusts him. The word is the one often used of trusting God. Achish puts his confidence in a man who is deceiving him, while David has stopped speaking of trust in the LORD at all.
passages.later:
The idiom of making oneself a stench goes back to Jacob, who told his sons, “You have brought trouble upon me by making me a stench to the Canaanites and Perizzites, the people of this land” (Genesis 34:30).

Proverbs names what this chapter shows: “Lying lips are detestable to the LORD, but those who deal faithfully are His delight” (Proverbs 12:22).
passages.hard:
How can the Bible's hero wipe out whole communities and lie to cover it?

The difficulty is real. David kills men and women alike, not in the heat of battle but to leave no witnesses, and he lies again and again. Readers have answered in several ways. Some note that the peoples named, the Amalekites above all, were under the ban declared against them (Exodus 17:14; chapter 15), so David's war on them fits an earlier command, though his motive in this chapter is secrecy and not obedience. Others stress that the narrator reports without approving. Scripture often tells what its heroes did without endorsing it, and the silence about prayer in this chapter hints that David is acting outside God's guidance. Still others see in David's deception a ruse of war of the kind ancient readers admired when the weak outwitted the strong.

Whatever view one takes, the chapter does not present David's conduct as a model. It shows the moral cost of a double life, and the cost begins to arrive in chapter 30, when the Amalekites strike Ziklag.

No one may use these verses to justify violence against any person or people. No people living today is Amalek, and the chapter has no nation, land or conflict of today in view.
passages.asks: David's double life worked, for a while. Ask whether you are living one face before one person and another before someone else. And ask what it would cost you to stop, and what it may cost you if you do not.
